Dell found a manifold on Thursday, on a scrapped ferry in a yard outside Halifax, and on Friday the yard sold it to somebody else.

"Outbid," Dell said on the phone. His voice was flat with anger. "Some outfit from Portland called an hour before me and paid triple. Triple, Wren, for a part off a dead boat. Who does that?"

She knew who did that. She hung up without saying goodbye.

The *Margaret Ann* sat at the end of the pier with a red Coast Guard tag zip-tied to her wheel. The sunset cruises were cancelled. The two charters Wren had booked for June had both called, apologetic and vague, to say their plans had changed; she did not ask who had made them change. The sixty-four thousand dollars sat in the Saltmarsh Savings and Loan, and it was a great deal of money, and it was not a hundred and twenty.

On Friday evening an envelope arrived by courier. Inside, on heavy cream paper, was Corwin Pell's original offer, freshly typed, with one change. The forgiveness of the debt now required her signature *before* the council vote on Monday. A yellow flag marked the line. A fountain pen had been helpfully included.

She put it on the desk under the green lamp.

Tobias came in at six with grocery bags and stopped when he saw it. "Tell me you're not."

"Look at the numbers, Toby."

"I don't care about the numbers."

"I *do*. That's the whole problem. Somebody in this family has to." She heard herself, and she hated how she sounded, and she kept going anyway. "The boat's grounded. The charters are gone. Pell owns the parts suppliers, the lawyers, probably half the council. If I sign, I walk away clean. I keep the house. I keep the boat. I run her from the town dock and nobody owes anybody anything."

"You keep a boat with no pier and no fuel and four feet of water at low tide." His voice rose. "Dad would never—"

"Dad *mortgaged the pier*." She was on her feet. "Dad borrowed a hundred and twenty thousand dollars from that man and didn't tell either of us, and then he went out in the dark and died and left me to clean it up. Like he left me to clean up after you."

The words sat in the air like smoke.

Tobias set the grocery bags down very carefully on the counter. A can of soup rolled out and he caught it and put it back. "Okay," he said quietly. "Okay. That's fair."

"Toby, I didn't—"

"No. You did. It's fair." He picked up his jacket. "I came back because you said you could use me. Turns out you've got it handled. You always did." He paused at the door. "Sign it if you want. It's your ledger."

The bell rang behind him.

Wren stood alone in the office. The lamp hummed. Out the window, the sodium light at the head of the pier came on, and under it she could see her brother walking away up Front Street with his hands in his pockets, getting smaller, not looking back, the way he had walked away ten years ago.

She sat down at the desk. She uncapped Corwin Pell's fountain pen. It was a beautiful pen, heavy and cold, and it fit her hand perfectly, as if it had been weighed for her.

She held it over the yellow flag for a long time.

Then she put the cap back on, and laid the pen down beside the paper, and put her face in her hands, and for the first time since March, Wren Halloway cried.
